source.title: Predictable Confabulations: Factual Recall by LLMs Scales with Model Size and Topic Frequency
source.authors: Matthew Smith; Jonathan P. Shock; Samuel T. Segun; I. E. Olatunji; Tegawendé F. Bissyandé

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a downstream factual-recall measure varies predictably with model scale, using generated scholarly references rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports factual-recall quality by model and scaling fits, so those outcomes bear on V6. Its discussion of Kaplan and Hoffmann is background, not a test of held-out loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation. The results concern scholarly-reference recall; they do not test other modalities or the other downstream tasks mentioned in V6.
record.test_reason: The study measures a downstream task, scholarly-reference recall quality, across 38 models. It fits how that quality varies with parameter count: log-linear across 16 dense models (R2=0.794), and a sigmoid that also includes topic frequency (R2=0.599). This bears on V6 in a new task setting. Its own results do not test held-out loss, allocation, architecture shape, other modalities or fit-dependence of loss laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that recall quality follows a sigmoid in log parameter count plus log topic representation (R2=0.599 on 16 dense models) and generalises across 38 models. The fit has floor, ramp and ceiling regimes, and larger models extend recall into the citation tail. They frame confabulation as predictable and stress that the design is observational, with family offsets and about 40% of variance unexplained.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates generated scholarly references and fits recall-quality relationships to parameter count and an OpenAlex topic-frequency proxy. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, token-count scaling, training compute, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Recall-quality fit differs between the continuous authenticity × relevance metric and binary title-match metric (R2 = 0.599 versus 0.604; fitted coefficients also differ). Family-level intercept offsets are reported. The authors note the fixed prompt and temperature-0 setup, but do not test alternative prompts or decoding settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Recall quality rises with topic representation in training data (OpenAlex proxy): 37 of 38 models show positive Spearman ρ, median 0.55. Topic frequency adds 17.8% explained variance beyond size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream factual recall scales predictably with the training-data frequency of the concept, in addition to model size.

fits_no_version.finding: The median citation count of correctly recalled references falls with model size (slope −0.35, ρ=−0.79). Larger models recall further down the citation tail.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models extend factual recall into lower-frequency (long-tail) knowledge.

record.problems: The study is observational and cannot separate model size from correlated training differences or establish a causal effect of topic frequency. OpenAlex counts are an indirect proxy for opaque training data. The main sigmoid fit pools 16 dense models and 384 model-topic observations; the authors caution that treating these observations as independent understates uncertainty. Within-family fits use as few as three model sizes. Evidence is limited to English scholarly references and a fixed prompt; other factual domains and languages are untested.
record.rows_left_out: None of the separately reported model quality values in Table A3 were omitted. The paper states that per-model citation-count confidence intervals are plotted in Figure 5 but does not give their exact bounds in the text; only the expressly stated citation medians and aggregate fit are recorded.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling in parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of loss from small to large runs. The 50T-parameter estimate in the Discussion is an untested extrapolation of the recall fit, not loss.
Depth, width and architecture shape at fixed parameters. Dense vs MoE is compared only on total parameters, across differently trained models.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer regimes.
Predictability from pretraining loss. Scaling with tokens or compute. Tasks other than English scholarly-reference recall. Controlled scale sweeps: models differ in training data and recipe.
Fit-dependence of loss exponents or of the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Within-family log-linear fits: R2 0.74–0.94; slopes Mistral 0.218, Llama 0.224, Gemma 0.238, Qwen 0.366 (Qwen3 slope driven by floor-regime model)
Variance decomposition: log10 P alone explains 42.1% of variance; topic frequency adds 17.8% (F=169.6)
Relevance-weight sweep: sigmoid R2 ranges 0.504–0.606 and log-linear R2 0.481–0.573 as the PARTIAL weight varies
Verification categories by size within Llama: 405B 72% verified, 70B 63%, 8B 30%
MoE models underperform the dense sigmoid at equal total parameters

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T3: an existing-model cross-family evaluation of one downstream task, not a controlled scale sweep. Model size is confounded with training data and recipe. The first author co-founded SourceVerify, the scoring tool; the inter-rater check was done by the other authors. Per-model rows are only data points for the fits, so the verdicts rest on the aggregate fits.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs' held-out pretraining loss from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations, and their scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling in other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Tests factual recall of scholarly references, not other downstream tasks or predictability from pretraining loss.
The study compares two recall-quality metrics, but does not test setup-dependent exponents or compute-optimal splits for held-out loss scaling.

relationships.condition: Scholarly-reference recall quality across 16 dense models (1B–405B, four families), extending to 28 dense+MoE models on total parameters
relationships.reason: Quality rises log-linearly with parameter count (R2=0.794 dense, 0.712 with MoE). The sigmoid fit holds with similar R2 under a binary title-match metric (R39, R40, R41, R42).
relationships.display_finding: Recall quality increased log-linearly with parameter count, with R²=0.794 for dense models and 0.712 including MoE models, while binary title matching yielded similar sigmoid-fit R² values.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Scholarly-reference recall quality across 16 dense models (1B–405B, four families), extending to 28 dense+MoE models on total parameters
source_check.reason: Section 5.1 reports positive log-linear relationships with R2=0.794 and 0.712. Sections 5.3–5.4 report sigmoid R2=0.599 and binary-title-match R2=0.604.

relationships.condition: Across model families, training variants and the dense-vs-MoE comparison
relationships.reason: Same-size models differ by up to 0.23 in quality. Examples: Llama 8B 0.322 vs Qwen3 8B 0.054; 405B base 0.638 vs Hermes 0.703; Llama 3.1 vs 3.3 70B, 0.607 vs 0.446. Family intercepts shift, MoE models underperform the dense curve, and about 40% of variance is unexplained (R03, R04, R14, R15, R18, R19, R39, R41).
relationships.display_finding: Llama 8B scored 0.322 versus Qwen3 8B's 0.054, 405B base scored 0.638 versus Hermes's 0.703, and Llama 3.1 versus 3.3 70B scored 0.607 versus 0.446, while MoEs underperformed the dense curve and about 40% of variance remained unexplained.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Across model families, training variants and the dense-vs-MoE comparison
source_check.reason: Sections 4.6 and 5.1 document training-dependent quality and family offsets; Section 6 reports MoE underperformance relative to the dense sigmoid. Table A3 confirms the cited comparisons. The stated maximum difference of 0.23 is internally inconsistent: 0.322 minus 0.054 is 0.268.

relationships.condition: Floor and ceiling of the sigmoid, and the scoring choice
relationships.reason: Quality is sigmoidal, not a single log-linear law. Floor-regime models (e.g. Qwen3 8B) distort within-family slopes. Text-based: sigmoid R2 ranges 0.504–0.606 across relevance-weight choices (Table A6; rows R04, R41).
relationships.display_finding: Quality followed a sigmoid with floor and ceiling effects, with R² ranging from 0.504 to 0.606 across relevance weights and model rankings preserved at Spearman correlation of at least 0.997.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Floor and ceiling of the sigmoid, and the scoring choice
source_check.reason: V6 requires predictable improvement, without requiring a single log-linear form. The sigmoid predicts floor, ramp and saturation. Section 4.5 and Table A6 report robustness to relevance weights, preserving model rankings with Spearman rho at least 0.997; these results do not establish a scoring-dependent failure of V6.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
